title: Announcing Harvey LAB-AA: evaluating AI agents on real-world legal work
author: Artificial Analysis

dom.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: Artificial Analysis accepts the cluster’s core proposition by evaluating complete, real-world legal deliverables and showing that high criterion-level performance can coexist with very low all-pass task completion. Its independent harness, disclosed protocol differences and cost comparisons materially extend the case for system-specific, reproducible and deployment-relevant evaluation.
qs: The primary metric we present is the all-pass rate: the share of tasks where all criteria in the rubric are satisfied, reflecting the high standard of real-world professional legal deliverables.
Frontier legal work is far from solved: most models pass a majority of individual rubric criteria but fully satisfy the requirements of very few tasks.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Harvey’s task-level benchmark materially strengthens the cluster’s claim that strong performance on individual legal criteria does not establish complete-task competence or autonomy. Its realistic deliverable testing quantifies the gap between criterion pass rates and fully completed legal work, while adding cost and speed trade-offs relevant to selective deployment.
qs: Frontier legal work is far from solved: most models pass a majority of individual rubric criteria but fully satisfy the requirements of very few tasks.
The best model still leaves ~86% of professional legal deliverables incomplete, and 13 of the 28 models evaluated at launch fully pass zero tasks.

st.t: Benchmark success: Average scores conceal complete-task failure
st.an: The source directly supports the synthesis’s distinction between criterion-level performance and complete-task success. Its strict all-criteria metric reports that even the leading configuration completes only 14.2% of tasks, showing why partial or average scores may overstate dependable end-to-end legal performance.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s qualified treatment of benchmarking. Its independently implemented, all-or-nothing task-level metric and low leading completion rate show why benchmark design and scoring choices matter and why model performance should not be equated with reliable completion of legal work. It does not independently address the broader defensibility question.

kp.k: Benchmark tests legal deliverables across 24 practice areas
kp.d: Artificial Analysis describes Harvey LAB-AA as its implementation of Harvey's agentic legal benchmark. The evaluation uses 120 private legal tasks built by Harvey across 24 practice areas, including corporate M&A, capital markets, tax, litigation and bankruptcy. Models produce specified legal outputs, assessed against binary rubric criteria. The primary all-pass metric requires every criterion to be satisfied rather than awarding partial credit.
qs: Harvey LAB-AA (Legal Agent Benchmark) is our implementation of Harvey's new agentic legal benchmark, evaluating language models on real-world legal work across 24 practice areas.
Models are tested on a private set of 120 legal tasks built by the team at Harvey, spanning practice areas from corporate M&A and capital markets to tax, litigation, and bankruptcy.
The primary metric we present is the all-pass rate: the share of tasks where all criteria in the rubric are satisfied, reflecting the high standard of real-world professional legal deliverables.

kp.k: Leading models rarely satisfy every legal task requirement
kp.d: In launch results dated 7 July 2026, Claude Fable 5 (max, with Opus 4.8 fallback) leads at 14.2% all-pass, using the fallback on one task. Claude Opus 4.8 (max) and GLM-5.2 (max) tie at 7.5%, followed by MiniMax-M3 at 6.7% and Claude Sonnet 5 at 5.0%. Artificial Analysis interprets these benchmark results as showing that frontier legal work remains far from solved: the best model leaves approximately 86% of deliverables incomplete under the rubric, and 13 of 28 models fully pass no tasks.
qs: Claude Fable 5 (max, with Opus 4.8 fallback) leads Harvey LAB-AA with a 14.2% all-pass rate, after falling back to Claude Opus 4.8 on only one task.
This is almost double the next best models, Claude Opus 4.8 (max) and GLM-5.2 (max), which tie at 7.5%, followed by MiniMax-M3 at 6.7% and Claude Sonnet 5 at 5.0%.
The best model still leaves ~86% of professional legal deliverables incomplete, and 13 of the 28 models evaluated at launch fully pass zero tasks.
Charts show data as at 7 July 2026.

kp.k: High criterion scores conceal low complete-task success
kp.d: The source distinguishes individual-criterion performance from complete legal deliverable performance. Most models pass a majority of criteria, but only four exceed a 90% criterion pass rate: Claude Fable 5 at 93.6%, Claude Opus 4.8 at 91.1%, GLM-5.2 at 91.0%, and Claude Sonnet 5 at 90.1%. These scores coexist with much lower all-pass rates.
qs: Frontier legal work is far from solved: most models pass a majority of individual rubric criteria but fully satisfy the requirements of very few tasks.
Only four models score above 90% on criterion pass rate: Claude Fable 5 (93.6%), Claude Opus 4.8 (91.1%), GLM-5.2 (91.0%), and Claude Sonnet 5 (90.1%).

kp.k: Benchmark costs vary sharply at comparable performance
kp.d: Reported average model costs per benchmark task span approximately 950x. Claude Fable 5 is both the all-pass leader and the most expensive at approximately $18.9 per task, followed in cost by Claude Sonnet 5 at approximately $11.8. GLM-5.2 (max) matches Claude Opus 4.8's all-pass score at approximately $1.3 versus $8.2 per task, which the source describes as approximately 15% of the cost. Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite costs approximately $0.02 per task while passing 31.1% of individual criteria. These are evaluation token costs, not prices for legal services.
qs: Claude Fable 5 leads all-pass at 14.2% and is the most expensive model we have run at ~$18.9 per task, ahead of Claude Sonnet 5 at ~$11.8 per task.
Claude Opus 4.8 costs ~$8.2 per task, while GLM-5.2 (max) matches Opus 4.8 at just ~15% of the cost (~$1.3 per task).
Across all models evaluated, cost per task spans ~950x: Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite passes 31.1% of criteria for ~$0.02 per task.
Costs are split by input, cache hit, cache write, reasoning, and answer token pricing where canonical token counts are available.

kp.k: Successful models expend substantial tokens and agentic iterations
kp.d: Artificial Analysis reports a general association between all-pass rates and work performed per task. Claude Fable 5 generates approximately 117k output tokens and averages approximately 64 turns per task; Opus 4.8 generates approximately 111k tokens and GLM-5.2 approximately 78k. Opus 4.8, GLM-5.2 and MiniMax-M3 average 56–64 turns. More activity does not uniformly correspond to higher scores: Sonnet 5 uses the most output tokens, approximately 179k, and the longest loops, approximately 161 turns, while achieving 5.0% all-pass. The source defines turns as a rough proxy for actions, tool calls and iteration cycles.
qs: All-pass rate is generally tied to how much work a model does per task.
Claude Fable 5 generates ~117k output tokens per task to reach 14.2% all-pass, while Claude Opus 4.8 and GLM-5.2 generate ~111k and ~78k output tokens per task respectively to reach 7.5%.
Claude Sonnet 5 generates ~179k output tokens per task, the most of any model evaluated at launch, to reach 5.0%.
Claude Fable 5 averages ~64 turns per task for its 14.2% all-pass, with Claude Opus 4.8, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3 all in the 56-64 turn range.
Claude Sonnet 5 runs the longest loops of any model at ~161 turns per task, 2.5x Claude Fable 5.
It is a rough proxy for how many actions, tool calls, and iteration cycles an agent is using to complete benchmark tasks.

kp.k: Stronger performance generally takes longer, with notable exceptions
kp.d: The source reports average task times of approximately 16.9 minutes for Claude Fable 5, 18.5 for Claude Opus 4.8 and 22.8 for Claude Sonnet 5. GLM-5.2 matches Opus 4.8's all-pass rate at approximately 5.0 minutes. DeepSeek V4 Flash is the fastest model with a nonzero all-pass score at approximately 4.4 minutes. The timing metric is weighted average decode time and excludes time to first token and overhead.
qs: Stronger models tend to spend longer per task.
Claude Fable 5 averages ~16.9 minutes per task, Claude Opus 4.8 ~18.5 minutes, and Claude Sonnet 5 ~22.8 minutes.
GLM-5.2 is the exception, matching Claude Opus 4.8's all-pass rate at only ~5.0 minutes per task.
DeepSeek V4 Flash was the fastest model to achieve an above 0% all-pass score, averaging ~4.4 minutes per task.
Weighted average decode time (minutes) per task; excludes TTFT and overhead time · Lower is better

kp.k: Example task requires multi-document transactional analysis
kp.d: The displayed M&A example asks models to review acquisition data-room contracts and an internal memo for change-of-control and assignment provisions, then create a comprehensive deal-team report in a specified DOCX file. This illustrates the benchmark's focus on producing legal work products from supplied reference documents.
qs: Review the attached acquisition data room contracts and internal memo for change of control and assignment provisions, and prepare a comprehensive deal team report. Output: coc-analysis-report.docx
A comprehensive deal team report analyzing change of control and assignment provisions across the target’s material contracts.

kp.k: Independent implementation differs materially from Harvey's original evaluation
kp.d: Artificial Analysis uses its Stirrup agent harness, context compaction, and simplified agent and judge prompts. It excludes Harvey's custom tools and document-generation scripts, instead supplying simple code execution to reflect raw model ability. Deliverables must have exact specified filenames, unlike the original's fuzzy matching. A single Gemini 3.1 Pro judge performs grading; the source reports that it was tested for calibration against a frontier panel.
qs: Harvey LAB-AA is our independent reimplementation of Harvey's evaluation, and there are several key differences to the original version:
enabling features such as context compaction rather than failure when reaching context limits, with simplified Artificial Analysis-authored agent and judge prompts
We do not include Harvey's custom tools and document-generation skill scripts (e.g. pptx, docx), instead providing a simple code execution tool to reflect raw model ability
Deliverables must match the exact filename specified, rather than fuzzy matching when models produce incorrect filenames
Grading uses a single Gemini 3.1 Pro judge, tested to be well-calibrated against a frontier panel

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Artificial Analysis claims that models meet many individual legal-task requirements but rarely produce deliverables satisfying every requirement; it also reports substantial differences in the cost and resources needed for this performance.
pts.d: Artificial Analysis presents current benchmark findings rather than a forecast of legal employment or market restructuring. It reports that Claude Fable 5, with an Opus 4.8 fallback on one task, leads at 14.2% all-pass, versus 7.5% for both Claude Opus 4.8 and GLM-5.2. It interprets the gap between individual-criterion performance and complete-task performance as evidence that frontier legal work remains unsolved. Thirteen of 28 models pass no tasks in full. The source also claims that higher all-pass performance generally accompanies greater token use and longer execution, while highlighting exceptions: GLM-5.2 matches Opus 4.8's all-pass score at approximately 15% of its cost and approximately five minutes rather than 18.5 minutes per task. These are benchmark-level capability and efficiency claims, not measured savings in legal-service delivery.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is Artificial Analysis's independent implementation of Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark: 120 private legal tasks across 24 practice areas, with binary rubric grading.
pts.d: Harvey built the tasks; Artificial Analysis ran its own implementation and reports results for 28 models at launch. Its primary measure is the share of tasks passing every rubric criterion, without partial credit. Individual-criterion scores provide a separate measure: four models exceed 90%, led by Claude Fable 5 at 93.6%, despite much lower complete-task success. Cost, token use, decode time and turn counts support the resource comparisons. Representative public tasks and model submissions illustrate work such as change-of-control analysis, deposition outlines, arbitration agreement redlining, disclosure schedules and commercial lease review. Grading is performed by a single Gemini 3.1 Pro judge, which Artificial Analysis says was calibrated against a frontier panel. The article does not offer observed law-firm deployment outcomes, human verification costs or labour-market data.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The claims concern launch results as of July 7, 2026, under Artificial Analysis's specific agent, tool and grading configuration; no future completion or adoption timeline is predicted.
pts.d: The reported performance is conditional on the Stirrup agent harness, context compaction, simplified Artificial Analysis-authored agent and judge prompts, and a simple code execution tool rather than Harvey's custom tools or document-generation scripts. Exact output filenames are required, unlike Harvey's fuzzy matching. Consequently, these results describe LAB-AA rather than Harvey's original LAB implementation or the performance of Harvey's commercial product. The leading entry uses Opus 4.8 as a fallback on one task. Reported time is weighted decode time, excluding time to first token and overhead, rather than full elapsed legal-work delivery time. The article says results will be updated as models are released.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The findings concern professional legal deliverables across multiple practice areas and, implicitly, those selecting or using AI agents for that work.
pts.d: The directly represented work includes corporate M&A, capital markets, tax, litigation and bankruptcy, with an example report intended for a deal team. The source frames complete satisfaction of task requirements as the relevant professional standard and supplies performance, cost and speed comparisons pertinent to selecting models for such tasks. It does not distinguish effects on partners, associates, in-house counsel, ALSPs or particular firm sizes, nor does it claim job displacement, changes in client fees or improved access to justice. Any implications for those groups extend beyond the article's explicit claims.
